I doubt I'll be able to see anything, but I want an accurate estimate of whether the Moon is visible right now.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-04-14 12:21 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-04-14T12:21:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 34.122 degrees and its azimuth is 159.921 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 18.176 degrees and its azimuth is 200.971 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 11.39 percent illuminated, 39.356 degrees from the Sun, and 375827.9 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

**Probably not with unaided eyesight—though it is not physically impossible.**

The Moon is a **thin waning crescent**, only **11.4% illuminated**, and just **39.4° from the Sun**. Although it is **18.2° above the horizon**, Reykjavík’s bright daytime sky, plus the relatively low altitude and associated atmospheric haze/extinction, will greatly reduce its contrast. Its position about **41° west of due south** also places it roughly **36° to the Sun’s right and 16° lower**, which helps you aim but does not make the crescent conspicuous.

For an ordinary observer who only knows roughly where to look, I would rate the naked-eye chance as **low—perhaps around 10–25% under genuinely clear, transparent conditions**, and lower if there is haze or thin cloud. Knowing the exact position relative to a landmark could improve the odds substantially.

**Practical verdict:** expect **not** to see it unaided. It should be findable with binoculars, but because it is fairly near the Sun, use extreme care: stand where a building completely blocks the Sun and never sweep binoculars toward it. Once located binocularly, you might then manage to see it with the naked eye.
